claim: GSDMD and GSDME are the only GSDMs readily expressed in bone microenvironment.
source: Gsdmd and Gsdme were the only GSDM family members that were readily detected in BM and BM-free tibias from wild-type (WT) mice (Figure 1A–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and Western blot data from bone marrow and bone tissue samples shown in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: Expression levels of Gsdmd in BM and BM-free tibias were consistently higher in fractured compared with unfractured bones.
source: Expression levels of Gsdmd in BM and BM-free tibias (Figure 1A–C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) were consistently higher in fractured compared with unfractured bones.
evidence: Supported by qPCR and Western blot data comparing fractured and unfractured bones shown in Figure 1.

claim: Fracture injury did not affect Gsdme mRNA levels.
source: The injury did not affect Gsdme mRNA levels (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Fracture injury increased GSDME protein levels in BM-free tibias.
source: The injury did not affect Gsdme mRNA levels (Figure 1A) but it increased GSDME protein levels in BM-free tibias (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Both GSDMD and GSDME appeared constitutively cleaved in BM but not BM-free tibias.
source: Both GSDMs appeared constitutively cleaved in BM (Figure 1C–D) but not BM-free tibias (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing cleaved forms in BM samples but not in BM-free tibias.

claim: Gsdmd deficiency increased baseline Gsdme mRNA levels in BM-free tibias but not BM.
source: Gsdmd deficiency increased baseline Gsdme mRNA levels in BM-free tibias but not BM, a response that was unaffected by the injury and did not impact GSDME protein levels (Figure 1A–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and Western blot data comparing WT and Gsdmd-/- mice shown in Figure 1.

claim: Bone callus volume was significantly reduced in mice lacking either GSDMD or GSDME compared with wild-type mice.
source: The volume of bone callus was higher on day 14 compared with day 10 post-injury in WT mice (Figure 1E). It increased indistinguishably in Gsdmd-/- and Gsdme-/- mice on day 14 compared to day 10, but was significantly lower in mutants compared with WT mice (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT quantification and 3D reconstructions shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: Compound loss of GSDMD and GSDME did not exacerbate fracture healing outcomes compared to single mutants.
source: Notably, callus volume was comparable between single and compound mutants (Figure 1E–F), suggesting that both GSDMs share the same signaling pathway in fracture healing.
evidence: Supported by micro-CT data comparing single and double knockout mice shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: GSDMD and GSDME share the same signaling pathway in fracture healing.
source: Notably, callus volume was comparable between single and compound mutants (Figure 1E–F), suggesting that both GSDMs share the same signaling pathway in fracture healing.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that double knockout mice do not show worse phenotype than single knockouts.

claim: Callus bone volume increased linearly until day 14 post-fracture and plateaued by day 21 in WT mice.
source: Time-course studies revealed that while the callus bone volume increased linearly until day 14 post-fracture and plateaued by day 21 in WT mice (Figure 2A–B)
evidence: Supported by micro-CT quantification over time shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Callus volume continued to expand in Gsdmd-/- mice until day 21.
source: Time-course studies revealed that while the callus bone volume increased linearly until day 14 post-fracture and plateaued by day 21 in WT mice (Figure 2A–B), it continued to expand in Gsdmd-/- mice until day 21 (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT quantification over time shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Callus volume declined in both WT and Gsdmd-/- mice by day 28 but was larger in mutants compared with WT controls.
source: The callus volume declined in both mouse strains by day 28 but it was larger in mutants compared with WT controls (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT quantification at day 28 shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The areas of newly formed mesenchyme, cartilage, and bone were smaller in Gsdmd-/- compared with WT mice on day 7.
source: Histological analysis indicated that the areas of the newly formed mesenchyme, cartilage, and bone were smaller in Gsdmd-/- compared with WT mice on day 7 (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: Supported by histological quantification shown in Figure 2C-F.

claim: Cartilage remnants were negligible in WT callus on day 14 but remained abundant in Gsdmd-/- counterparts.
source: While cartilage remnants were negligible in WT callus on day 14, they remained abundant in Gsdmd-/- counterparts (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The number of osteoclasts declined after day 14 in both WT and Gsdmd-/- bones.
source: Additional histological assessments revealed that the number osteoclasts, which are involved in the remodeling of the newly formed bone, declined after day 14 not only in WT bones as expected, but also in mutants (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: Supported by TRAP staining and quantification shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: There were more osteoclasts in injured Gsdmd-/- bones compared to WT counterparts at any time-point.
source: At any time-point, there were more osteoclasts in injured Gsdmd-/- bones compared to WT counterparts.
evidence: Supported by TRAP staining quantification shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: Injured WT tibias exhibited decreased strength and stiffness compared with unfractured counterparts.
source: Injured WT tibias exhibited decreased strength and stiffness compared with unfractured counterparts (Figure 3A–C), indicating that the healing response has not fully recovered bone function at this time-point.
evidence: Supported by biomechanical torsion testing data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Fractured bones from Gsdmd-/- mice exhibited lower biomechanical parameters compared with WT controls.
source: Notably, fractured bones from Gsdmd-/- mice exhibited lower biomechanical parameters compared with WT controls.
evidence: Supported by biomechanical torsion testing data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The functional competence of the repaired bone structure is compromised in GSDMD-deficient mice.
source: Thus, the functional competence of the repaired bone structure is compromised in GSDMD-deficient mice.
evidence: Inferred from biomechanical testing showing reduced strength, stiffness, and toughness in fractured Gsdmd-/- bones.

claim: Baseline secretion levels of IL-1β and IL-18 were comparable between WT and Gsdmd mutants.
source: Baseline secretion levels of IL-1β or IL-18 were comparable between WT and Gsdmd mutants (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data from unfractured bone marrow supernatants shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Fracture increased IL-1β and IL-18 levels in BM supernatants in both WT and Gsdmd-/- mice.
source: Fracture increased IL-1β and IL-18 levels in BM supernatants in both groups, but they were significantly attenuated in mutant samples compared with WT controls (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data from fractured bone marrow supernatants shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Fracture-induced IL-1β and IL-18 levels in BM were significantly attenuated in Gsdmd-/- mice compared with WT controls.
source: Fracture increased IL-1β and IL-18 levels in BM supernatants in both groups, but they were significantly attenuated in mutant samples compared with WT controls (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data comparing WT and Gsdmd-/- mice shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Baseline levels of Il1b and Il18 mRNA were undistinguishable between WT and Gsdmd-/- samples in both BM and BM-free bone compartments.
source: Baseline levels of Il1b and Il18 mRNA were undistinguishable between WT and Gsdmd-/- samples in both compartments (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from unfractured samples shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: Following fracture, the expression of Il1b and Il18 mRNA was induced in WT but not Gsdmd-/- mice.
source: Following fracture, the expression of Il1b and Il18 mRNA was induced in WT but not Gsdmd-/- mice (Figure 4C–D), suggesting a feedback mechanism whereby these cytokines secreted though GSDMD pores amplified their own expression.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data comparing fractured WT and Gsdmd-/- samples shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: IL-1β and IL-18 secreted through GSDMD pores amplify their own expression through a feedback mechanism.
source: Following fracture, the expression of Il1b and Il18 mRNA was induced in WT but not Gsdmd-/- mice (Figure 4C–D), suggesting a feedback mechanism whereby these cytokines secreted though GSDMD pores amplified their own expression.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that cytokine mRNA expression is induced in WT but not Gsdmd-/- mice after fracture.

claim: Fracture increased the expression of Nlrp3 and Aim2 in WT and mutants only in BM-free bone samples.
source: Fracture increased the expression of Nlrp3 and Aim2 in WT and mutants only in BM-free bone samples (Figure 4C–D)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from BM-free bone samples shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: Fracture induced caspase-1 expression in WT cells in both BM and BM-free bone compartments.
source: Fracture increased the expression of Nlrp3 and Aim2 in WT and mutants only in BM-free bone samples (Figure 4C–D) whereas it induced caspase-1 expression in WT cells both compartments.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The expression of Nlrc4 and caspase-11 mRNA was not modulated by fracture injury or loss of GSDMD.
source: Never was the expression of Nlrc4 and caspase-11 mRNA modulated by the fracture injury nor loss of GSDMD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The abundance of neutrophils, monocytes, and macrophages in BM of uninjured bones was unaffected by loss of GSDMD.
source: Flow cytometry analysis revealed that the abundance of these cells in BM of uninjured bones was unaffected by loss of GSDMD (Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from unfractured bones shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Fracture increased the percentage of neutrophils and monocytes but not macrophages.
source: Fracture increased the percentage of neutrophils and monocytes but not macrophages (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data comparing unfractured and fractured bones shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: GSDMD deficiency was associated with a slight decrease in the percentage of neutrophils and increase in monocytes.
source: GSDMD deficiency was associated with a slight decrease and increase in the percentage of neutrophils and monocytes, respectively (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data comparing WT and Gsdmd-/- mice shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: ATP levels were comparable between WT and Gsdmd-/- samples at baseline but were induced by fourfold after fracture in both groups.
source: ATP levels were comparable between WT and Gsdmd-/- samples at baseline but were induced by fourfold after fracture in both groups (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by ATP assay data from bone marrow supernatants shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Bone particles were as potent as nigericin and ATP in inducing GSDMD cleavage by LPS-primed macrophages.
source: Bone particles were as potent as the NLRP3 inflammasome activators, nigericin and ATP, in inducing GSDMD cleavage by LPS-primed macrophages (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data from in vitro macrophage experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Nigericin, ATP, and bone particles induced IL-1β release by macrophages through mechanisms involving GSDMD.
source: Accordingly, these danger signals induced IL-1β release (Figure 5F) and pyroptosis as assessed by the release of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH; Figure 5—figure supplement 3A), responses that were attenuated in GSDMD-deficient macrophages.
evidence: Supported by ELISA and LDH assay data from in vitro macrophage experiments shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Nigericin and ATP robustly stimulated GSDMD cleavage and IL-1β release by LPS-primed neutrophils through mechanisms that partially involved GSDMD.
source: Both nigericin and ATP robustly stimulated GSDMD cleavage and IL-1β release by LPS-primed neutrophils through mechanisms that partially involved GSDMD, but they did not promote neutrophil pyroptosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot, ELISA, and LDH assay data from in vitro neutrophil experiments shown in Figure 5G-H and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Nigericin and ATP did not promote neutrophil pyroptosis.
source: Both nigericin and ATP robustly stimulated GSDMD cleavage and IL-1β release by LPS-primed neutrophils through mechanisms that partially involved GSDMD, but they did not promote neutrophil pyroptosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by LDH assay data from in vitro neutrophil experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Bone particles had no effect on GSDMD maturation and IL-1β and LDH release by neutrophils.
source: Bone particles had no effect on GSDMD maturation and IL-1β and LDH release by neutrophils (Figure 5G–H and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot, ELISA, and LDH assay data from in vitro neutrophil experiments shown in Figure 5G-H and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Bone callus volume was larger on day 14 compared with day 10 in WT and Il1r1-/- tibias.
source: Bone callus volume was larger on day 14 compared with day 10 in WT and Il1r1-/- tibias, but it was smaller at both time-points in mutants compared to WT controls (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT quantification shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Bone callus volume was smaller in Il1r1-/- mice compared to WT controls at both day 10 and day 14.
source: Bone callus volume was larger on day 14 compared with day 10 in WT and Il1r1-/- tibias, but it was smaller at both time-points in mutants compared to WT controls (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT quantification shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: The mesenchyme, cartilage, and bone areas were all smaller in Il1r1-/- compared with WT mice.
source: Histological analysis confirmed that the mesenchyme, cartilage, and bone areas were all smaller in Il1r1-/- compared with WT mice (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: Supported by histological quantification shown in Figure 6C-F.

claim: Cartilage remnants were prominent within the callus of Il1r1-/- specimens at day 14.
source: Like in Gsdmd-/- tissues, cartilage remnants were prominent within the callus of Il1r1-/- specimens at day 14 (Figure 6F)
evidence: Supported by histological images shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The number and surface of osteoclasts were significantly higher in Il1r1-/- compared to WT mice at day 14.
source: Like in Gsdmd-/- tissues, cartilage remnants were prominent within the callus of Il1r1-/- specimens at day 14 (Figure 6F), and the number and surface of osteoclasts were significantly higher at all times in mutant compared to WT mice at day 14, while cartilage and bone areas remained smaller in mutants at day 10 (Figure 6G–I).
evidence: Supported by TRAP staining quantification shown in Figure 6G-I.

claim: Il1r1-/- mice exhibited delayed fracture healing like Gsdmd-/- mice.
source: Although Gsdmd expression was not analyzed in Il1r1-/- mice, these mutants exhibited delayed fracture healing like Gsdmd-/- mice, suggesting that functional GSDMD-IL-1 axis is important for adequate bone healing after fracture.
evidence: Supported by comparison of phenotypes between Il1r1-/- and Gsdmd-/- mice shown in Figures 2 and 6.

claim: Functional GSDMD-IL-1 axis is important for adequate bone healing after fracture.
source: Although Gsdmd expression was not analyzed in Il1r1-/- mice, these mutants exhibited delayed fracture healing like Gsdmd-/- mice, suggesting that functional GSDMD-IL-1 axis is important for adequate bone healing after fracture.
evidence: Inferred from the similar phenotypes of Gsdmd-/- and Il1r1-/- mice in fracture healing.

claim: Amino-terminal fragments from proteolytically cleaved gasdermins form plasma membrane pores that enable the secretion of IL-1β and IL-18.
source: Amino-terminal fragments from proteolytically cleaved gasdermins (GSDMs) form plasma membrane pores that enable the secretion of interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and IL-18.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gasdermin function cited in the introduction.

claim: Excessive GSDM-mediated pore formation can compromise the integrity of the plasma membrane thereby causing pyroptosis.
source: Excessive GSDM-mediated pore formation can compromise the integrity of the plasma membrane thereby causing the lytic inflammatory cell death, pyroptosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gasdermin function cited in the introduction.

claim: Bone fractures are one of the most frequent injuries of the musculoskeletal system.
source: Bone fractures are one of the most frequent injuries of the musculoskeletal system.
evidence: This is general knowledge about bone fractures stated in the introduction.

claim: Delayed healing, compromised quality of newly regenerated bone, or nonunions remain frequent outcomes of bone fractures.
source: Despite advances in therapeutic interventions, delayed healing, compromised quality of the newly regenerated bone, or nonunions remain frequent outcomes of these injuries (Clement et al., 2013; Muire et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Fracture outcomes are complicated by advanced age, infection, or sterile inflammation-prone comorbidities such as rheumatoid arthritis or diabetes mellitus.
source: These outcomes are complicated by the advanced age of the patients, infection, or sterile inflammation-prone comorbidities such as rheumatoid arthritis or diabetes mellitus (Clement et al., 2013; Muire et al., 2020; Claes et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The recovery speed from fracture is greater in small animals such as rodents than in large counterparts and humans.
source: Although the recovery speed from fracture is greater in small animals such as rodents than in large counterparts and humans, the underlying repair mechanisms are shared across species (Claes et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The underlying repair mechanisms of fracture healing are shared across species.
source: Although the recovery speed from fracture is greater in small animals such as rodents than in large counterparts and humans, the underlying repair mechanisms are shared across species (Claes et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Bone fracture triggers an immediate inflammatory response during which neutrophils and macrophages are mobilized to the injury site.
source: Bone fracture triggers an immediate inflammatory response during which neutrophils and macrophages are mobilized to the injury site to remove necrotic cells and debris while releasing factors that initiate neovascularization and promote tissue repair by recruiting mesenchymal progenitor cells from various sites such as the periosteum and bone marrow (BM) (Claes et al., 2012; Colnot et al., 2006; Glass et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The repair phase is followed by remodeling events where the balanced activity of osteoblasts and osteoclasts culminates in the restoration of the original bone structure and BM cavity.
source: The repair phase is followed by remodeling events where the balanced activity of osteoblasts and osteoclasts culminates in the restoration of the original bone structure and BM cavity (Colnot et al., 2006; Hardy and Cooper, 2009; Xing et al., 2010b).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Inflammation subsides during fracture healing stemming from the suppressive actions of immune cells such as regulatory T cells, anti-inflammatory macrophages, and mesenchymal stem cells.
source: Ultimately, inflammation subsides stemming from the suppressive actions of immune cells such as regulatory T cells, anti-inflammatory macrophages, and mesenchymal stem cells (Al‐Sebaei et al., 2014; Nauta and Fibbe, 2007; Noël et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mice lacking IL-6, TNF-α, or macrophages exhibit defective fracture healing.
source: Although inflammation declines over time, interfering with its onset immediately after injury can be detrimental as mice lacking interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor-α, or macrophages exhibit defective healing (Yang et al., 2007; Wallace et al., 2011; Gerstenfeld et al., 2003; Baht et al., 2015; Raggatt et al., 2014; Xing et al., 2010a; Chang et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A fine-tuned level of inflammation is critical for adequate fracture healing.
source: Thus, a fine-tuned level of inflammation is critical for adequate fracture healing.
evidence: Inferred from studies showing that both excessive and insufficient inflammation impair healing.

claim: IL-1β is an inflammatory cytokine that impacts fracture healing.
source: IL-1β is another inflammatory cytokine that impacts fracture healing (Einhorn et al., 1995; Morisset et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: IL-1β and IL-18 lack the signal peptide for secretion through the conventional endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi route.
source: Unlike the aforementioned cytokines, IL-1β and IL-18 lack the signal peptide for secretion through the conventional endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi route.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IL-1β and IL-18 secretion.

claim: Pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 are proteolytically activated by enzymes such as caspase-1.
source: Expressed as pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18, these polypeptides are proteolytically activated by enzymes such as caspase-1, a component of the intracellular macromolecular complexes called inflammasomes (Schroder and Tschopp, 2010; Broz and Dixit, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Caspase-1 cleaves GSDMD, generating GSDMD amino-terminal fragments which form plasma membrane pores.
source: Caspase-1 also cleaves GSDMD, generating GSDMD amino-terminal fragments, which form plasma membrane pores through which IL-1β and IL-18 are secreted to the extracellular milieu (Broz and Dixit, 2016; Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Live cells can secrete IL-1β and IL-18 through GSDMD pores.
source: Although live cells can secrete these cytokines, excessive GSDMD-dependent pore formation compromises the integrity of the plasma membrane, causing a lytic form of cell death known as pyroptosis (Shi et al., 2015; Evavold et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pyroptotic cells release IL-1β, IL-18, and other inflammatory molecules including eicosanoids, nucleotides, and alarmins.
source: Pyroptotic cells release not only IL-1β and IL-18 but also other inflammatory molecules including eicosanoids, nucleotides, and alarmins (Broz and Dixit, 2016; Shi et al., 2015; Rauch et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: GSDM family proteins are encoded by Gsdma1-3, Gsdmc1-4, Gsdmd, and Gsdme (also known as Dnfa5) in the mouse genome.
source: GSDMD is a member of the GSDM family proteins, which are encoded by Gsdma1-3, Gsdmc1-4, Gsdmd, and Gsdme also known as Dnfa5 in the mouse genome (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Mice lacking GSDMD are protected against multi-organ damage caused by gain-of-function mutations of NLRP3 or pyrin inflammasome.
source: Mice lacking GSDMD are protected against multi-organ damage caused by gain-of-function mutations of nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-like receptors family, pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) or pyrin inflammasome (Xiao et al., 2018; Kanneganti et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: GSDMD is involved in the pathogenesis of complex diseases including experimental autoimmune encephalitis, radiation-induced tissue injury, ischemia/reperfusion injury, sepsis, renal fibrosis, and thrombosis.
source: GSDMD is also involved in the pathogenesis of complex diseases including experimental autoimmune encephalitis, radiation-induced tissue injury, ischemia/reperfusion injury, sepsis, renal fibrosis, and thrombosis (Li et al., 2019; Xiao et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019; Silva et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021c; Zhang et al., 2021a).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: GSDME harbors overlapping and non-overlapping actions with GSDMD, depending on cell contexts.
source: GSDME is of particular interest to this study because recent evidence suggests that it harbors overlapping and non-overlapping actions with GSDMD, depending on cell contexts.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: GSDME can mediate pyroptosis and release cytokines under both GSDMD sufficient and insufficient conditions.
source: Indeed, GSDME can mediate pyroptosis and release cytokines under both GSDMD sufficient and insufficient conditions (Wang et al., 2021; Xia et al., 2021; Aizawa et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The role that gasdermins play in fracture healing has not been studied prior to this work.
source: Despite advances in GSDM studies, the role that these proteins play in fracture healing has not been studied.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study.

claim: Drugs for the treatment of GSDM-dependent inflammatory disorders and cancers are under development.
source: Since drugs for the treatment of GSDM-dependent inflammatory disorders and cancers are under development, it is imperative to understand their functions in the musculoskeletal system.
evidence: This is general knowledge about drug development stated in the introduction.

claim: Loss of GSDMD or GSDME in mice impeded fracture healing through mechanisms involving IL-1 signaling.
source: Here, we found that loss of GSDMD or GSDME in mice impeded fracture healing through mechanisms involving IL-1 signaling.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by data from multiple experiments.

claim: Drugs that inhibit GSDM functions may contribute to unsatisfactory fracture healing outcomes.
source: This discovery has translational implications as drugs that inhibit GSDM functions may contribute to unsatisfactory fracture healing outcomes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: When stabilized with an intramedullary inserted pin, fractured murine long bones heal through mechanisms that involve the formation of callus structures.
source: When stabilized with an intramedullary inserted pin, fractured murine long bones heal through mechanisms that involve the formation of callus structures (Marsell and Einhorn, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Biomechanical properties of unfractured Gsdmd-/- tibias were slightly higher though not statistically significant compared with WT unfractured bones.
source: Biomechanical properties of unfractured Gsdmd-/- tibias were slightly higher though not statistically significant in Gsdmd-/- compared with WT unfractured bones (Figure 3A–C), findings that were consistent with the higher bone mass phenotype of Gsdmd-/- mice relative to their littermates (Xiao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by biomechanical testing data shown in Figure 3A-C and citation to previous work.

claim: Gsdmd-/- mice have a higher bone mass phenotype relative to their littermates.
source: Biomechanical properties of unfractured Gsdmd-/- tibias were slightly higher though not statistically significant in Gsdmd-/- compared with WT unfractured bones (Figure 3A–C), findings that were consistent with the higher bone mass phenotype of Gsdmd-/- mice relative to their littermates (Xiao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: GSDMD is cleaved by caspase-1, caspase-11, neutrophil elastase and cathepsin G, or caspase-8.
source: This outcome was unexpected because these GSDMs are activated via distinct mechanisms as GSDMD is cleaved by caspase-1, caspase-11 (mouse ortholog of human caspase-4 and -5), neutrophil elastase and cathepsin G, or caspase-8 whereas GSDME is processed by caspase-3 and granzyme B (Zhang et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: GSDME is processed by caspase-3 and granzyme B.
source: This outcome was unexpected because these GSDMs are activated via distinct mechanisms as GSDMD is cleaved by caspase-1, caspase-11 (mouse ortholog of human caspase-4 and -5), neutrophil elastase and cathepsin G, or caspase-8 whereas GSDME is processed by caspase-3 and granzyme B (Zhang et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Caspase-11 is the mouse ortholog of human caspase-4 and -5.
source: This outcome was unexpected because these GSDMs are activated via distinct mechanisms as GSDMD is cleaved by caspase-1, caspase-11 (mouse ortholog of human caspase-4 and -5), neutrophil elastase and cathepsin G, or caspase-8 whereas GSDME is processed by caspase-3 and granzyme B (Zhang et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about caspase nomenclature.

claim: Functional complementation of GSDMD by GSDME has been reported.
source: Furthermore, functional complementation of GSDMD by GSDME has also been reported (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: IL-1α and IL-1β play an essential role in bone repair.
source: This view was consistent with the reported essential role of IL-1α and IL-1β in bone repair and aligned with the high expression of these cytokines by immune cells, which are known to massively infiltrate the fracture site (Claes et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Immune cells massively infiltrate the fracture site.
source: This view was consistent with the reported essential role of IL-1α and IL-1β in bone repair and aligned with the high expression of these cytokines by immune cells, which are known to massively infiltrate the fracture site (Claes et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: IL-1 signaling induces the expression of cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors that govern bone remodeling.
source: IL-1 signaling induces the expression of cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors that govern bone remodeling, a process that is initiated by the osteoclasts (Kitazawa et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Bone remodeling is a process that is initiated by osteoclasts.
source: IL-1 signaling induces the expression of cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors that govern bone remodeling, a process that is initiated by the osteoclasts (Kitazawa et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Loss of GSDMD in mice resulted in increased bone mass at baseline as the result of decreased osteoclast differentiation.
source: Consistent with the critical actions of GSDM-IL-1 cascades in bone repair and the osteoclastogenic actions of IL-1β, loss of GSDMD in mice resulted in increased bone mass at baseline as the result of decreased osteoclast differentiation (Xiao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Bone marrow is the site of hematopoiesis in adult animals.
source: This view is based by the fact that BM is the site of hematopoiesis in adult animals and vascularization is important for the traffic of osteoclast progenitors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bone marrow function.

claim: Vascularization is important for the traffic of osteoclast progenitors.
source: This view is based by the fact that BM is the site of hematopoiesis in adult animals and vascularization is important for the traffic of osteoclast progenitors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bone biology.

claim: Disruption in either hematopoiesis or vascularization should impact osteoclastogenesis.
source: As a result, disruption in either hematopoiesis or vascularization should undoubtedly impact osteoclastogenesis (Buettmann et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature and logical inference.

claim: The inflammasome-GSDM pathways are functional in the osteoblast lineage.
source: Although our mechanistic studies revolved around myeloid cells from which the osteoclasts arise, it is worth noting that the inflammasome-GSDM pathways are functional in the osteoblast lineage (Zhang and Wei, 2021b; Lei et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Osteoblast lineage autonomous actions of inflammasome-GSDM pathways in bone healing cannot be ruled out.
source: Therefore, osteoblast lineage autonomous actions of these pathways in bone healing cannot be ruled out.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential mechanisms not directly tested in the study.

claim: Disulfiram inhibits the processing or functions of GSDMD and GSDME.
